theme: The bread of life, sovereign grace and discipleship
readingInstruction: Read John 6:1-71. Jesus feeds the five thousand, walks on the sea, and then teaches in the synagogue at Capernaum that he is the bread of life. Many disciples leave. Notice the tension between God’s drawing and the human response.
settingTheScene: It is near Passover, and a great crowd has followed Jesus because of his signs. The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that appears in all four Gospels. John uses it as a sign pointing to Jesus himself. The long discourse that follows is one of the most challenging in the Gospel, and it ends with a crisis of belief.
observation: “Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated” (6:11).
“It is I; do not be afraid” (6:20).
“This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (6:29).
“I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (6:35).
“All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (6:37).
“No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day” (6:44).
“Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (6:53).
“Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (6:68).
interpretation:
Jesus tests Philip with a question about where to buy bread for the crowd. Andrew finds a boy with five barley loaves and two fish. Jesus gives thanks, distributes the food, and everyone eats their fill, with twelve baskets left over. The crowd wants to make him king by force, and he withdraws. That night he walks on the sea to the disciples in the storm, saying, “It is I; do not be afraid.” The Greek is “I am,” the divine name.

The crowd finds him the next day, looking for more bread. He says, “You are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill.” They ask what work they must do, and he says that the work of God is to believe in the one he sent. They ask for a sign like the manna that Moses gave. Jesus says the true bread from heaven is a person: “I am the bread of life.” The one who comes to him will never hunger, and the one who believes will never thirst.

Then he speaks of the Father’s work. “All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.” Here is the double truth of salvation. The Father gives, and the Son receives. Everyone given will come, and no one who comes will be turned away. “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” Salvation begins with God. And yet the invitation is real: “whoever comes.” Reformed Christians have found in this chapter a clear statement of God’s sovereign grace, and all Christians find in it a promise that Jesus will not reject anyone who comes.

The talk of eating his flesh and drinking his blood scandalizes the crowd. Jesus is speaking of feeding on him by faith, as the following verses make clear: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help.” Christians have also seen in these words a connection to the Lord’s Supper. Many disciples turn back and no longer walk with him. Jesus asks the Twelve, “Do you want to go away also?” Peter answers for them: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.” Peter does not understand everything, but he knows there is no one else.
connection: Exodus 16 is the manna in the wilderness. Psalm 78:24-25 speaks of the bread of heaven. Isaiah 55:1-3 invites the hungry to come and eat. Deuteronomy 8:3 says man does not live by bread alone. Matthew 14:13-33 is the parallel to the feeding and the walk on water. 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 and 11:23-26 speak of the bread of the Lord’s Supper. Ephesians 1:4-5 and Romans 8:29-30 speak of God’s choosing.
application:
Ask what you are hungry for. Are you coming to Jesus for his gifts or for himself?

Rest in verse 37: if you have come to Jesus, he will never cast you out.

When doctrine is hard, say Peter’s words: “Lord, to whom shall we go?”
prayerPrompts: Tell Jesus what you hunger for, and thank him that he is the bread of life.
Thank him that whoever comes to him he will never cast out.
Ask him to keep you from turning away.
